content: Settings that lack the capacity to perform phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) face challenges in implementing advanced diagnostic methods. Current next-generation sequencing (NGS) systems have limitations, particularly in terms of the computational expertise and resources required. These systems are typically more suitable for national tuberculosis (TB) reference laboratories (NTRLs) and high-performing regional TB reference laboratories. Amplification-based targeted NGS assays have been developed to detect drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) directly from sputum samples. One such assay, the Deeplex-MycTB assay (manufactured by GenoScreen, Lille, France), is commercially available in both CE-IVD and research-use-only (RUO) versions. This assay can predict resistance to 15 anti-TB drugs with a turnaround time of less than 48 hours. Diagnostic tests with World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations, such as those using compact devices like the MinION handheld sequencer, offer potential advantages. However, these assays have not yet been reviewed or approved by WHO for clinical use. A significant issue with these technologies is the lack of a standardized and robust single reference source for interpreting mutations. To address this, WHO has developed guidance and released a comprehensive catalog of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and their associations with drug resistance. This catalog, which includes data from over 38,000 MTBC isolates with matched phenotypic DST and whole genome sequences, is the largest of its kind and will be regularly updated. It is also expected to support the development of other rapid molecular DST methods. In resource-limited or high-burden settings, TB laboratory networks often follow a pyramidal structure. At the peripheral level (Level I), basic diagnostic tests such as lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear microscopy, and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) like Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra, and Truenat MTB are performed. These tests are suitable for initial TB detection and rifampicin resistance testing. However, LF-LAM is limited to use among people living with HIV (PLHIV) who meet specific criteria and lacks drug-resistance detection capabilities. At the intermediate level (Level II), laboratories require more sophisticated infrastructure and expertise. Technologies such as moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), line-probe assays (LPAs), and culture-based methods may be implemented. Reliable and rapid sample transport systems are essential to connect peripheral laboratories to intermediate and central laboratories. Centralized testing can be cost-effective in low-burden settings or where skilled staff shortages exist. At the central level (Level III), advanced testing requiring highly skilled personnel, infrastructure, and biosafety precautions is conducted. This includes whole genome sequencing, phenotypic DST for new and repurposed drugs, and troubleshooting discordant results. Central laboratories also play a key role in quality assurance, training, and surveillance. The implementation of new diagnostic tests requires careful planning, including reviewing WHO policies, defining the intended use of the test, updating national diagnostic algorithms, and conducting situational analyses of laboratory capacities. A phased implementation plan with clear targets and timelines should be developed, supported by financial and human resource commitments. Specimen referral systems are critical to optimizing access to services, ensuring timely testing, and maintaining quality assurance. The predictive value of diagnostic tests depends on the prevalence of TB in the population being tested. False-negative results can lead to missed treatment opportunities, while false-positive results may result in unnecessary treatment. Countries must consider trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity when selecting tests for implementation. Additionally, multi-disease testing platforms can improve efficiency and cost-effectiveness, particularly in settings with low diagnostic volumes for individual diseases. In summary, the successful implementation of TB diagnostic tests requires a well-coordinated approach involving stakeholders, robust infrastructure, and adherence to WHO guidelines.
